notes: Edit fixes a real inversion. Source (corpus/stories/PT005-the-jackal-and-the-war-drum.txt line 10; also corpus/panchatantra_complete.txt line 1648): "Now when the drum was struck by the tips of grasses swaying in the wind, it made the sound, but was dumb at other times." The pre-edit line "quiet when the wind blew" contradicted this; new lines 15-19 ("quiet when the wind was still / When the wind blew, the grass swayed and struck the drum / That was what made the sound") now match. The 9+ sibling (corpus/age/9+/PT005...txt line 7) states the same correct causality, confirming a 4-9-only defect now repaired. Remaining telling tracks source events: hungry jackal hears a great sound and is dejected (source lines 6-8); spies war-drum and asks who made it; creeps near believing it stuffed with meat and fat; gnaws hole and enters; finds only wood and skin; laughs (source lines 10-24). No invented events. Surrounding text coherent (line 13 "loud noise" then the lines 15-19 explanation). Moral "Don't judge something by its noise or appearance" is a faithful paraphrase of the source resolution "one should not be troubled by a mere sound" (line 30). No new defect left by the edit.

FAITHFUL. The single edit replaced only the moral line. Old moral ("Trusting no one can lead to trouble") was inverted relative to source: Godly "trusted no man, and kept his treasure under his arm by night and day" — his distrust PROTECTS the treasure; the loss occurs only when he entrusts the robe (with the treasure) to June at the river, after which "June seized the treasure and decamped." New moral ("Trusting a false friend can lead to trouble") matches that mechanism and the source's own frame, where the teller concedes "in introducing this grass-nibbler to the master you were handling live coals" and laments "we, when tricked by June." Body (lines 3-55) tracks the source beat-for-beat with no invented events: holy man with treasure, rogue June, wall/door obstacles, befriending, "Glory to Shiva," request for a vow, sleeping outside the cell, initiation, June's scheming to kill, the pupil's invitation, the river, the entrusted robe, the theft. Line 55 flows coherently into the new moral; no incoherence or new defect introduced. No source line is contradicted.

Edit changed "You can fly away, but I will drown." to "You can fly away, but the water is drying up." Source: turtle is "a water-dweller, and here I should perish very quickly from the scant supply of water"; "as the water dries in this lake... to me it means immediate death." Old line invented drowning (impossible in a dried lake, inverts the mechanism); new line states the source's actual danger. Edit is corrective and faithful. All actors and events match the source (Shell-Neck; ganders Slim and Grim; twelve-year drought; stick-grip plan; silence warning; flight over city; the "cartlike object" question; falls; cut to bits by meat-seekers). Moral "Always listen carefully to good advice" matches the source's embedded verse "To take advice from kindly friends." The chapter's hand-off is only the outer-frame transition to PT022 (Forethought, Readywit, and Fatalist); PT021 is fully resolved within the chapter. Surrounding text remains coherent; no new defect introduced.

The edit correctly repairs the telling. Before the edit the telling invented a mechanism (Right-Mind asking the goddess to "come out," the voice refusing, magistrates "looking inside the tree") that appears nowhere in the source. The new text restores the source's actual causal chain, matching corpus/panchatantra_complete.txt lines 5828-5830 exactly: "Right-Mind heaped inflammable matter about the hole in the mimosa and set fire to it. As the mimosa burned, Wrong-Mind's father issued from the hole with a pitiful wail, his body scorched..." / "'It is all Wrong-Mind's doing,' he replied." Actors and events now match: the father is hidden in the tree (source line 5814/5826: he speaks from his hole in the mimosa), Right-Mind burns the tree, the scorched father confesses. The moral ("Think carefully before doing something") reflects the father's warning (source line 54-64: "This is no kind of a scheme... Wise thought must first reveal"). Surrounding text (lines 53-69) stays coherent through the edit: voice from the tree -> fire -> father runs out -> confession -> trick exposed. The only divergence from source is the softened outcome (telling: "Wrong-Mind had to give back the stolen money"; source line 5830: he was hanged and Right-Mind received royal favor). That is acknowledged age-appropriate content-softening for a 4-9 audience, not a fabricated event, and not citable as an invented event or wrong moral. No defect raised.

The source fable (corpus/stories/PT041-self-defeating-forethought.txt, lines 6-49) is self-contained: hillman shoots boar, boar kills him, both die; a jackal finds them and plans to eat the sinew at the bow-tip "very slowly," then "the gut snapped, the bow-tip pierced the roof of his mouth... And the jackal perished from the pain of it." The chapter's terminal hand-off ("And Gold told the story of") is the outer frame, so no continuation lookup is needed for this fable. The applied edit replaced the invented, self-contradictory cause ("the jackal's greed made him eat too quickly") with "as he ate, the bowstring snapped. The bow-tip went into his mouth," which matches the source mechanism exactly and is coherent with the preceding line 17 that keeps the jackal's slow-eating plan. Actors, actions, and the greed moral all match the authority text; the edit introduced no new defect. Minor unresolved wart (pre-existing, untouched by this edit, not raised as a defect): line 3 opens "Two hunters were once out in the forest" and line 11 says "the hunter" singular, whereas the source has a single hillman ("There was once a hillman in a certain place"). This is a scene-setter count artifact only; no second hunter ever acts and no event changes, so it does not alter the depicted story.

Edit is faithful and corrects a real error. Source (Ryder 1925, corpus/stories/PT042-mister-duly.txt line 86; duplicated at corpus/panchatantra_complete.txt line 7700): "Then the king promised immunity to one and all, arrived at the truth by piecing their narratives together, and ended by respectfully giving Mister Duly his own daughter, together with a thousand villages." Lines 74-84 show the princess, the policeman's daughter, and the merchant's daughter each speak in turn. The old telling line credited MD with saving all three women — the source saves only the bride (merchant's daughter); the princess (source line 50) and Naughty (source line 58) each dismiss and send him away, which the telling's own body already showed at lines 15 and 19. The new text ("The princess, the policeman's daughter, and the merchant's daughter told their tales. The king heard them all. He learned the truth.") faithfully paraphrases "arrived at the truth by piecing their narratives together." No invented events; actors and actions match; moral ("What's duly yours, you will receive" vs source "What's duly his, a man receives") is correct; surrounding text stays coherent (king learns truth -> gives daughter and villages). Minor pre-existing, non-edit wording at line 15 ("But when the prince spoke, she realized he was not the one she loved") is readable as the princess's mistaken label for the visitor and does not rise to a defect; noted only, not raised.

Both edits verified against the authoritative source. Edit 1: telling now reads "We must find a way to stay safe," matching source line 10 where the mice convene over their OWN survival ("We are being killed... Therefore let us devise a remedy effective in this crisis") rather than an invented motive to help elephants. Edit 2: "He remembered the mice. They were his only hope." matches source line 28 ("We have no means of deliverance except those mice") where the king recalls the mice as his sole means of deliverance, not as prior benefactors. All actors and events track the source: mice in a decayed settlement, elephant-king crushes mice, survivors meet, delegation asks the king to spare them, he grants it, later he is trapped, recalls the mice, sends an elephant-cow, mice gnaw the ropes and free the herd. Surrounding text remains coherent after both edits (self-preservation motive -> "Please don't hurt us"; "only hope" -> sending the elephant-cow). No invented events and no new defect. Moral "Make friends with everyone, big or small" faithfully renders the source refrain at corpus/panchatantra_complete.txt:8546 ("Make friends, make friends, however strong / Or weak they be: Recall the captive elephants / That mice set free"). The mice story is self-contained within the source chapter (resolution at source line 32), so no hand-off resolution lookup was required.

The applied edit (Gold "the deer" -> "the mouse") is correct and complete. Source authority: the chapter's closing verse names the four friends "The deer and turtle, mouse and crow," and corpus/panchatantra_complete.txt line 664 states the Book II framing tale is the friendship of "the crow, the mouse, the turtle, and the deer, whose names are Swift, Gold, Slow, and Spot" — so Gold is unambiguously the mouse (and Swift the crow, Slow the turtle, Spot the deer). The correction also removes a self-contradiction: the very next scene has Gold slip into a grass-clump and the source has Gold describe himself as "a little fellow" who will "find some chink to slide into" — a mouse action, inconsistent with the old "deer" label. Surrounding text stays coherent: "Slow, the turtle, was caught by the hunter. Gold, the mouse, came up with a plan to save him. They told Spot to pretend to be dead, and Swift to pretend to peck out Spot's eyes" reads cleanly, with "him" = Slow and "They" = the friends. All other beats match Ryder's source: Spot the deer caught in the snare, gifted to the prince, treated with ointments/massage/baths/food/perfumes/salves; the verse quoted verbatim ("When shall I follow on the herd / Of coursing deer again? / When brace myself against the wind / That whistles by? Ah, when?"); the prince terrified thinking it a prodigy/magic deer; sorcerers and magicians summoned; the holy man's reassurance and the prince's release; Slow the turtle caught and bound; Gold's plan (Spot feigns death by water, Swift pecks at his eyes); hunter throws the turtle down and runs for a club; Spot escapes, Swift flies into a tree, turtle reaches the water, Gold into a grass-clump; hunter confused and flees; four friends free and happy. Moral ("True friends help each other in times of need") fits the source's "The Winning of Friends." No invented events; no NEW defect introduced.

Both edits verified faithful against corpus/stories/PT056 (Ryder) and the true resolution in corpus/panchatantra_complete.txt (hand-off at ch end resolved at line 11628: the spared suppliant guest, Live-Strong, later exterminates Foe-Crusher). Edit 1 fixes the inverted thief condition — source: "Should I want a thing, I'll return if she does not Passionately cling" → telling: "I will come back when she does not hug you." Correct, and it removes the fabricated "'Maybe I should not kill him. He helped us.'" thought (nowhere in source). Edit 2 fixes the frame: source has Flame-Eye ("advantage may be anticipated from a benefactor, thief though he be... he should not be killed") and Hook-Nose ("he should not be killed") — telling's "His counselors said the guest should not be killed. Help may come from a benefactor, even a thief" matches. Actors/events all correct: Lovelorn marries young girl; thief enters at night; wife clings in fear; old man thanks thief and offers goods; thief declines. Moral ("Help from unexpected people can be very useful") summarizes the source verdict. No new incoherence introduced — the compressed frame's un-introduced "guest" predates the edit and is supported by the source ("How much more from a suppliant guest?"), so no source line is contradicted.

The edit restores the fable's true resolution and is source-faithful. Source chapter ends on a hand-off (stories/PT068 line 28, "And the king told the story of"); the real closing beat is corpus/panchatantra_complete.txt:12375 — "Just so you, too, had best decamp before these veterans learn that you are a potter. If not, you will be hooted and killed." And the potter, hearing this absconded. The new line 27 ("You must go too, before they find out you are a potter. If not, they will hoot you and kill you." The potter heard this and ran away.) is a faithful condensation: same actors (king, potter), same event (potter flees), no invented event/dialogue; the "too" is source-grounded ("Just so you, too"). Every other beat matches the source chapter (careless potter, broken pot, famine, joins guards, king's misplaced honor, jealous princes, army review, name/family question, Fight-Firm confession, king's shock, dismissal, plea, refusal). The 9+ sibling carries the same resolution, confirming the fix. Surrounding text stays coherent and the removed meta line "but it's not important right now" was correct to cut. Checked the moral (line 29, "Honesty is always the best policy"): it differs from the source frame-narrator's cynical maxim ("who lets the truth slip out, like Fight-Firm, he is sure to lose his victory," complete.txt:12274-12280), but the recorded defect for this item was solely the missing resolution (data/certification_2026-10-13.json:406-411), the cert pass flagged no 4-9 moral defect (unlike PT033 9+), and the plain events — an honest confession leading to safe flight — support the positive moral at the 4-9 level. Not a citable defect, so not flagged. No new defect introduced.

The source chapter (corpus/stories/PT073-the-farmer-s-wife.txt) ends on a hand-off — "How was that?" asked the crocodile. And the monkey told the story of [line 78] — so I traced the frame's true resolution in corpus/panchatantra_complete.txt.

Every beat of the edit matches the source:
- Monkey's refusal: telling line 29 "You are foolish. I will not give you advice." = source "I will not tell you a thing... because you took your wife's advice and carried me out to sea" (line 12678).
- Monkey relents and advises fighting: telling line 31 "But at last the monkey helped him. He told the crocodile to be brave and fight for his home." = source "Well, well, my good fellow, I advise you to go and fight him" (line 12700) plus "put his reliance in resolute valor" (line 12820).
- Crocodile wins his home back: telling line 33 "He fought the other crocodile and won. He got his house back and lived there happily." = source "he joined battle with the desperate ruffian who had forced a way in... killed him. So he recovered his home and lived there happily for a long time" (line 12820).

Same actors (monkey, crocodile), no invented events. The moral "Bad things often happen together" is the source's own frame reflection "How true it is that misfortunes never come singly!" (line 56). Coherence check: the edit cleanly removes the previously dangling "a monkey who broke a sparrow's nest" (a story the telling never told) and the transition from refusal (line 29) to relenting (line 31) reads cleanly; no new defect introduced. The earlier farmer's-wife / she-jackal material (telling lines 5-23) also tracks source lines 6-44 (rogue takes money and clothes, she-jackal loses meat and fish, mutual "as unlucky as" exchange). No contradicting source line found.

The edit corrects an invented event. Source (corpus/stories/PT077-ill-considered-action.txt): "Then the barber conducted them well into the house and clubbed them. Under the clubbing some died, others had their heads broken and began to bawl." Only Jewel's fate-sent monk turned to gold; the monastery monks did not. The edited line "He clubbed them, but they did not turn to gold" matches the source and is consistent with the telling's next line ("They saw the monks running with blood," matching "blood streaming over their bodies"). All actors and events in the telling (Jewel of Trumpet-Flower, the dream of the Jain monk/trillion dollars, the doubting proverb, the barber manicuring the wife's nails, the striking with a stick, the barber's greedy plan, soldiers, court, judges condemning the ill-advised act) trace to the source. Moral ("Think before you act") matches Book V's frame: "Ill-advised leave unbegun... Take a warning from the barber." The chapter's trailing hand-off ("they told the story of the lady and the mungoose") is a transition to the next tale, not this story's resolution. No incoherence or new defect introduced by the edit.

Source: corpus/stories/PT083-slow-the-weaver.txt. The edit removed the invented outcome sentence "The people learned a lesson.", leaving "Slow died." followed by the Moral line. Grep confirms neither "lesson" nor "learn" occurs in the source chapter, so the deleted sentence asserted an outcome the source never states. Surrounding text is coherent; no dangling fragment, and the following Moral line still reads cleanly.

All actors and events match the source: weaver Slow (broken loom pegs), trip to the seashore for wood, the sissoo tree whose fairy begs to spare her home and offers any boon, the barber friend who urges asking for a kingdom ("You can be king, and I will be prime minister"), the wife who advises a second pair of arms and an extra head, Slow's request, his transformation into a two-headed/four-armed being, and the townspeople beating him to death as a fiend. No invented events.

The chapter ends on a hand-off ("And the other told the story of"), but that is the frame's transition to the next tale, not a continuation of Slow's; Slow's story is genuinely complete at his death, so nothing is truncated.

Moral "Ask for what you really need, not what looks nice" is a faithful simplification of the source's verses against extravagantly high hopes; not contradicted by any line. Only nit (not raised as a defect, cannot cite a contradicting source line): "Slow's wife was not at home." is a minor connective invention — the source never states she was absent, and he in fact reaches her shortly after — but it is pre-existing, does not derive from this edit, and does not contradict a specific source line.

The applied edit removed the invented closing sentence pair ("Seedy woke up, and his friends laughed at him. He looked silly with his white face."). Source corpus/stories/PT084-the-brahman-s-dream.txt line 10 ends the story at the whitening ("...the barley-meal which it contained turned him white all over."); the chapter's trailing "And the other told the story of" is a hand-off to a separate tale (King Moon), not part of PT084. corpus/panchatantra_complete.txt line 13565 confirms no waking, friends, or laughter exists — the Brahman is solitary. Post-edit the telling ends at "Seedy turned white from head to toe." then the Moral, so the surrounding text is coherent, nothing dangles, and no new defect was introduced. All remaining beats (Seedy, jar of barley-meal on a peg, famine/100 rupees, goats/cows/buffaloes/mares, great house, lovely daughter, son Moon-Lord, stable roof, jump from mother's lap to knee, wife too busy, the kick smashing the jar, whitening) map to the source; the moral is a fair age-4-9 rendering of Ryder's "Do not indulge in hopes" / "Greedy folk who do not heed / Consequences of a deed." Faithful.

Edit correctly fixes the attribution inversion. Source line 40 has the counselors en masse give the twelve-year grammar-then-religion curriculum; source line 42 has Keen alone propose the epitome. The current telling (lines 9-11) now matches exactly: advisors say "It will take twelve years," and "one advisor, Keen" proposes "a summary of the essential facts." Surrounding text is coherent — line 13's "the king liked Keen's idea... this summary" follows naturally. Downstream content (land-grant offer, name-forfeit, five books, six months) still matches source lines 54/56/60. No new defect introduced; actors and events unchanged. Chapter has no hand-off ending, so corpus/panchatantra_complete.txt was not needed.

The edited line 5 ("The driver told Increase that Lively had sunk in the mud.") now matches the source exactly: at stories/PT003 line 56 the driver reports only that "Lively was wearied by the trip, and sank in the mud," and the false death report is given to "the men" at line 60 — which the telling itself preserves on line 7 ("The men, fearing the forest's dangers, made a false report that Lively had died."). The edit removes the prior internal contradiction (driver + men both reporting death) and introduces none: line 5 -> line 7 read coherently. The chapter ends on a hand-off ("And Cheek told the story of", line 106), so I checked the continuation in corpus/panchatantra_complete.txt. The telling's remainder faithfully condenses it: Rusty's proud, uneducated character (complete lines 68-98); the jackals' estrangement scheme (line 2568); Victor's two lies — to Rusty that Lively "plan[s] to kill him and to seize the royal power" (line 3399) and to Lively that the lion has "treachery in mind" (lines 4115/5141); the battle and killing (lines 5277, 6267); and Rusty's lament "Lively was almost my second life. In killing him, I have only hurt myself" (line 6267, telling renders "was my second life"). The moral "Greed and malice can lead to the loss of true friends" matches the source's opening verse, "A jackal then estranged the friends / For greedy and malicious ends" (lines 14-16). No invented events; same actors doing the same things. The sprawling nested stories are dropped as age-appropriate condensation, not fabrication.

The edit correctly restores the source's role inversion. Source (corpus/stories/PT006-merchant-strong-tooth.txt): "Now Bull received the two garments as if they were the Kingdom of Heaven, and feeling intense satisfaction, he said: 'Friend merchant, I forgive you.'" The telling now reads "Bull was overjoyed and said, 'Friend, I forgive you.'" — Bull, the wrongdoer, magnanimously forgives Strong-Tooth; the prior "apologized for his actions" was the defect and is gone. Surrounding text stays coherent: Strong-Tooth explains why he drove Bull out (source: "It was because I saw you... sitting where you did not belong, that I humiliated you"), then Bull forgives him, matching source order and Bull's deluded magnanimity. All other beats match the source: wedding and escort of the king; Bull's false accusation of kissing the queen; king withdrawing favor; Strong-Tooth attributing it to Bull; the next day's absurd second claim about the king ("When our king sits at stool, he eats a cucumber"); king reinstating Strong-Tooth "with gems from his own person and with garments." Moral ("A little thing can lift someone high, and a little thing can bring them down") matches the source proverb ("A little thing will lift him high, A little make him fall"). The Strong-Tooth tale resolves within this chapter, so no hand-off lookup in panchatantra_complete.txt was needed. No new defect introduced and no defect left. Non-blocking pre-existing note (not introduced by this edit, not a hard source contradiction): the telling calls Bull "jealous of Strong-Tooth's position" where the source attributes his motive to humiliation ("the humiliation so rankled in Bull's inner soul" after Strong-Tooth "administered a cuffing and drove him out") — a characterization softening, though the telling still says Strong-Tooth "had driven him out."

defects.claim: The edit shifted the subject of the sentence to Godly ('June served Godly, but Godly still did not trust him.'), so the immediately following sentence 'He thought of killing Godly' now resolves 'He' to Godly, yielding the self-contradictory 'Godly thought of killing Godly.' In the source it is June, not Godly, who reflects on killing Godly. The edit fixed the distrust actor but left the pronoun antecedent pointing at the wrong actor.
defects.source_quote: June reflected: "Dear me! Do what I will, he does not trust me. So shall I kill him with a knife in broad daylight? Or give him poison? Or butcher him like a beast?"

notes: Everything else is faithful: same actors, same events (monastery, garments-for-money, rogue June, win-trust-and-discipleship plan, 'Glory to Shiva. Amen', the caste-changing prayer, the vow and the warning not to enter the cell at night, the pupil's son's invitation, the river, the handed-over treasure, June fleeing with it). The source ends on a full resolution ('June seized the treasure and decamped'), not a hand-off, so no chase into corpus/panchatantra_complete.txt was needed. No explicit moral in either text, so none to fault. The single defect is the coherence break introduced by this edit: telling line reads 'Godly still did not trust him. He thought of killing Godly, but then a pupil's son arrived...' Fix by disambiguating the pronoun, e.g. 'As time passed, June served Godly, but Godly still did not trust him. June thought of killing him, but then...' The rationale in the edit (Godly is the distrusting party) is itself correct per the source and should be kept.

confirmedDefects.claim: The edit shifted the subject of the sentence to Godly ('June served Godly, but Godly still did not trust him.'), so the immediately following sentence 'He thought of killing Godly' now resolves 'He' to Godly, yielding the self-contradictory 'Godly thought of killing Godly.' In the source it is June, not Godly, who reflects on killing Godly. The edit fixed the distrust actor but left the pronoun antecedent pointing at the wrong actor.
confirmedDefects.reason: Confirmed. Telling line 13 reads: 'June served Godly, but Godly still did not trust him. He thought of killing Godly, but then a pupil's son arrived...' The subject of the immediately preceding independent clause is Godly, so the default antecedent for 'He' is Godly, giving the incoherent 'Godly thought of killing Godly.' The source (corpus/panchatantra_complete.txt line 2219) clearly attributes the reflection to June: 'As the time passed in this manner, June reflected: "Dear me! Do what I will, he does not trust me. So shall I kill him with a knife in broad daylight? Or give him poison? Or butcher him like a beast?"' The source's structure is also contrastive-correct: 'he does not trust me' (June speaking, Godly = 'he') whereas the telling inverted who distrusts whom and then left the pronoun pointing at the wrong actor. The telling contradicts the source and is internally self-contradictory.

defects.claim: The telling's moral runs opposite to the source's lesson. The source moral is that sharing your home with a stranger is what destroyed Creep (Leap, the guest, is the agent of the host's ruin); the telling instead prescribes the reverse remedy -- being a mindful, boundary-respecting host. The body does not support the telling's moral either: Creep is the courteous host who scolds Leap and lays down the very boundary (the condition) and still dies, so good/boundary-setting hosting is not shown to avert the disaster. Source's own frame calls Creep's hospitality her undoing ('she agreed, since courtesy was her hobby').
defects.source_quote: With no stranger share your house; Leap, the flea, killed Creep, the louse.  (corpus/panchatantra_complete.txt:3868; chapter corpus/stories/PT015-leap-and-creep.txt:52 reads 'With no stranger share your house, . . . .')

notes: The listed edit is applied correctly and is a genuine improvement: the condition now exactly matches source line 44 ("When the king is drunk, tired, or asleep, then you may quietly bite him on the feet. That is the right time and place." vs source "When the king's body is mastered by wine, fatigue, or sleep, then you may quietly bite him on the feet. This is the right place and the right time."), removing the old self-contradiction. No new defect or incoherence is introduced by the edit -- the following line ("However, Leap misunderstood the condition and bit the king on the back when he was dozing off") still reads, though "misunderstood" is loose for what the source calls a deliberate violation of the agreed PLACE. All actors and actions match the source (Creep the host, Leap the guest who bites the back while the king dozes, king's servants killing Creep and her family instead of Leap); no invented events. The sole defect is the pre-existing moral, which the 2026-10-13 certification pass itself flagged as running "opposite to the source's lesson" and explicitly deferred to human judgment (it did not score it because the outcome, a host suffering, is depicted in the body and so did not fit the MORAL_UNEARNED category). That judgment was left open, and the correct call against the source authority is that the moral is unfaithful.

confirmedDefects.claim: The telling's moral runs opposite to the source's lesson; source says sharing your home with a stranger destroyed Creep (the guest is the host's ruin), while the telling prescribes the reverse remedy (be a mindful, boundary-respecting host), and the body does not support the telling's moral either since Creep sets the boundary and still dies.
confirmedDefects.reason: Source moral at corpus/panchatantra_complete.txt:3868 reads 'With no stranger share your house; Leap, the flea, killed Creep, the louse' — the lesson is that admitting the stranger (guest Leap) is what killed the host Creep. The source frame (line 3904) explicitly names hospitality as her undoing: 'she agreed, since courtesy was her hobby.' The telling (corpus/age/9+/PT015-leap-and-creep.txt:15) inverts this: 'Being a good host means being mindful of your guests' needs and respecting their boundaries, lest you suffer the consequences' — prescribing the opposite remedy. The telling's body also fails to support that moral: Creep scolds Leap (line 5) and lays down the boundary/condition (line 9), yet still dies (line 11), so boundary-respecting hosting is not shown to avert the disaster. The source clearly contradicts the telling's moral.

notes:
The edit fixed the prior defect cleanly. Current line 7 now matches the source exactly: lion (Haughty) fights an elephant, takes a tusk wound, keeps to his cave, and after five or six days of food failure tells the companions he cannot supply the usual food and orders them to hunt up a creature to be food "for you and myself" (source corpus/stories/PT018-ugly-s-trust-abused.txt lines 12-16). The earlier invented "fell ill / couldn't hunt / refused because on a diet" is gone; the "on a diet" phrase in the source (line 24) is the JACKAL's words to the lion, not the lion's excuse, so removing it from the lion is correct.

Surrounding text stays coherent: line 9 (jackal/crow plot; jackal proposes to Haughty; Haughty hesitant re his promise) follows from line 7's order to hunt; line 11 (jackal persuades re voluntary offering; crow/jackal/leopard each offer), line 13 (Ugly's speech), line 15 (lion gives the word, others tear him apart) all track source lines 18-149. No duplicated/leftover sentences from the edit.

Moral ("Those who live by their wits often end up being devoured by their own cleverness") is a loose but non-contradictory paraphrase of the source verse "All who live upon their wits... Do the wrong as quick as right... Camel, crow, and other creatures" (complete text lines 4408-4418); no source line states the opposite, so not raised as a defect.

Both applied edits are confirmed correct against Ryder's text. (1) Moral: source verse (panchatantra_complete.txt:5186-5189) reads "The wise who wrongs another, / Pursuing selfish good, / Should keep his plans a secret, / As Smart did in the wood" — the new moral ("Those who wrong others for their own good should keep their plans a secret, as Smart did") is a faithful paraphrase; the replaced karma line promised an eventual punishment the fable never delivers (Smart prospers, eating the meat slowly).
